# R359 — layer-major prefill weight-I/O prior art and transfer bounds

Date: 2026-10-13 (Asia/Tokyo). Read-only literature and closed-report review. No source edit, import/AST, test, build, GPU, profiler, process/service/reset, or Git operation. Only this report was written. The current registry path supplied for deduplication was absent in this environment; the closed R45/R71/R219 reports were available and reviewed. This is an applicability and byte-bound report, not a benchmark result.

## Finding

There is solid prior art for coupling layer-major/block schedules to reuse a layer's weights across a multi-token work unit. There is no external result found that measures this exact Strata Qwen3.8-Flash-Next/SYCL path, or that validates its stateful GDN/QSA/Ple semantics. In the current Strata scope, a full-prefix layer-major pass with one 512-expert cache per active layer would send each layer's packed expert set once, then reuse it over the 8K internal tiles. That changes the transfer count from a chunk-major schedule that reloads the layer for every tile to one fill per layer. It does not reduce below the one-fill-per-layer bound unless the routed union omits experts, or some complete weight bytes are already resident. The 64K amortization is plausible in byte arithmetic, but not yet a measured throughput claim.

This distinction matters because the older local report R219 describes a layer-major route that already loads all expert blobs once per layer across its configured chunks. It therefore cannot support claiming that a further within-layer weight-load saving exists on that route. The proposed layer-major whole-prefix scheduling opportunity is relative to the presently described chunk-major path in the task brief; route identity and actual transfer receipts must be checked in the current run before attributing savings.

## Primary implementation and paper evidence

- **FlexGen (ICML 2023, primary paper and authors' repository):** the block schedule co-schedules weights, activations and KV across GPU/CPU/disk. The paper states that a larger block leaves activation/KV I/O per token unchanged while proportionally reducing weight I/O per token; the diagonal schedule loads each layer's weights once per diagonal. It also explains that memory capacity and KV layout constrain the schedule. This is a schedule-level precedent, not a MoE-expert or Strata measurement. The evaluated workload is primarily autoregressive generation; its block size is not equivalent to Strata's 8K prefill tile. [Paper, PMLR ICML 2023](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/sheng23a/sheng23a.pdf), [authors' source](https://github.com/FMInference/FlexGen). The paper's layer weight I/O statements are at lines 1251–1287 and its non-contiguous-KV implementation issue at 1304–1310 of the PDF text.
- **ZeRO-Inference (DeepSpeed author design blog, 2022):** streams weights layerwise, keeps the layer output on GPU as the next layer's input, and uses the freed space to fit long sequences or larger batches. It separately discusses overlapping next-layer fetch with current-layer compute. It establishes layerwise activation residency as an implementation pattern, but its examples and evaluation are dense Transformer generation on V100 and do not prove MoE prefill reuse or Strata numerical compatibility. [DeepSpeed design post](https://www.deepspeed.ai/2022/09/09/zero-inference.html), [official example source](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeedExamples/tree/master/inference/huggingface/zero_inference). Post date: 2022-09-09.
- **Fiddler (ICLR 2025, paper and authors' repo):** the MoE-specific system dynamically chooses CPU-compute versus GPU-transfer plans by workload shape. Its paper explains that small inputs can favor moving activations to CPU for CPU expert compute, while larger inputs/batches can make the CPU too slow and favor transferring weights to GPU. This supports choosing by input shape and measured service costs, not a blanket rule that weight transfer or CPU execution always wins. It is a different model family/runtime/GPU and does not present this layer-major full-prefix schedule as a Strata result. [ICLR 2025 paper](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/8cd1ce03ea58b3d7dfd809e4d42f08ea-Paper-Conference.pdf), [authors' implementation](https://github.com/efeslab/fiddler). Publication date: ICLR 2025.
- **Anemll Flash-MoE, author-maintained implementation note/source (retrieved 2026-10-13):** a close practical analogue deduplicates selected experts across a prompt slab, reads each unique expert once for that layer/slab, and reuses it for all token references; it describes read-ahead batches and a per-expert routed-reference microbatch. Its listed examples and measurements are on Apple M5 Max and SSD, so only the algorithm is relevant here. It explicitly limits reuse to one layer and one slab, not across slabs. [Implementation note and source links](https://github.com/Anemll/anemll-flash-llama.cpp/blob/master/docs/flashmoe-layer-major-dedup-single-sidecar.md). The note has no publication date visible in the reviewed page; retrieved 2026-10-13.
- **SGLang/vLLM scope check:** SGLang's CPU roadmap distinguishes prefill CPU GEMM/cache blocking from sequential/pipelined GPU–CPU MoE offload; the projected 50–80% is a roadmap estimate, not a measured gain transferable to this host. vLLM's layerwise offload RFCs found in search concern KV-cache offload, not reducing expert-weight sends. These are not candidates for the specific claim here. [SGLang roadmap issue #8281](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/8281), [vLLM layerwise KV RFC #48203](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/48203).
- **PowerInfer:** excluded as a direct analogue. Its primary design keeps hot neurons from dense FFNs resident and computes cold neurons on CPU; that changes the offload unit and model structure, so its transfer reductions do not establish whole-expert MoE prefill savings. [SOSP 2024 paper](https://ipads.se.sjtu.edu.cn/_media/publications/song-sosp24.pdf), [authors' source](https://github.com/SJTU-IPADS/PowerInfer).

## Conditional I/O arithmetic for this machine

Inputs supplied by the task: 48 layers, 512 experts/layer, expert arena 46.84 GiB, residual width 10,240 FP32 values/token (40,960 bytes/token), 8K current tile, B570 installed PCIe Gen4 x4 encoded ceiling 7.8769 GB/s. The historical application rate near 6 GB/s is not a current route verification. I use decimal GB/s for rates and binary GiB for capacities. No model trace or actual request byte counter was obtained.

Assume a full layer fill copies the full 46.84 GiB packed expert arena once per request, evenly attributable across layers only for aggregate arithmetic. Then the request weight payload is about 50.29 GB. Its ideal serialized time is 6.39 s at the encoded link ceiling, or 8.38 s at the historical 6 GB/s scenario. Real transfer time can be longer; source reads, staging, synchronization and compute are excluded. This is a fixed one-fill lower bound across prompt lengths, conditional on the arena figure representing exactly the copied blobs.

If every layer boundary writes the entire FP32 prefix residual to host and reads it back for the next layer, 47 boundaries cost 94 full-plane transfers. That yields:

| Actual prefill tokens | One residual plane | Boundary residual traffic | + one full expert fill | 1000-token/s time budget | Serialized traffic at 6 GB/s | At 7.8769 GB/s |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 32,768 | 1.25 GiB | 117.5 GiB (126.16 GB) | 164.34 GiB equivalent | 32.77 s | 29.41 s | 22.40 s |
| 65,536 | 2.50 GiB | 235 GiB (252.33 GB) | 281.84 GiB equivalent | 65.54 s | 50.45 s | 38.15 s |
| 262,144 | 10 GiB | 940 GiB (1,009.32 GB) | 986.84 GiB equivalent | 262.14 s | 176.60 s | 127.21 s |

The “combined GiB equivalent” converts the 46.84-GiB weight fill to the same binary unit and adds it to residual traffic; time columns divide combined decimal bytes by the named link-rate scenario. These are serialized payload floors only. Overlap could hide some transfer under compute, while host staging, waits, attention/state traffic and other copies add cost. The 1000-token/s column is just tokens divided by the requested target; it is not an expectation that the path can reach that speed.

At 64K the one-time weights amortize to about 0.77 MB/token, while the residual boundary traffic is 3.85 MB/token. At 32K the weight share is about 1.54 MB/token, and at 256K it is about 0.19 MB/token. Therefore the 64K case does amortize a fixed once-per-layer weight fill over enough tokens for its ideal time (8.38 s at 6 GB/s) to be materially smaller than the 65.54 s target budget. But the residual-plane boundary traffic alone has a 42.05 s serial floor at 6 GB/s; weight plus this traffic accounts for about 77% of the budget before all computation and staging. At 256K the same conditional pair accounts for 67% of the 262 s budget. These fractions show feasibility pressure, not achieved TPS.

The current 8K chunk-major loop across all 48 layers can cause a layer's experts to be requested again in each tile. A layer-major schedule that computes each layer over all prompt tiles while holding its packed layer cache through those tiles removes that repeated-fill multiplier: ideal weight payload falls from up to tiles-times-full-arena to one full-arena fill. If considering only ceil(N/8192) tile count, the factors are 4x, 8x and 32x at 32K, 64K and 256K. This is only the upper structural ratio for full-set fills. Actual chunk-major transfer bytes can be lower if its route/cache serves only a subset, and actual layer-major bytes can be lower if only the selected union is copied. The layer-major design has an approximately 1.2-GB one-layer device cache and a 2.66-MB largest individual blob; these fit as stated relative to one another but do not establish real allocator headroom alongside workspaces and long-context state.

## Application boundary and next useful discriminator

This is especially state-sensitive: GDN recurrent/convolution state and QSA causal attention/indexer state advance along token order. A layer-at-a-time traversal can preserve each layer's chronological order, but an activation tile taken through all layers changes schedule/state ownership and repeats layer fills. Holding all-prefix residuals in host RAM at layer boundaries preserves the layer-major order and weight reuse, at the cost of the residual PCIe traffic above. A tiled schedule must name which of those two traversal orders it uses; “tile activations” alone does not imply both fewer weight sends and fewer residual transfers.

Minimum evidence for any implementation comparison: current baseline route receipt; actual bytes sent per layer/chunk and unique routed-expert union; one cache fill and cache lifetime receipt; total boundary H2D/D2H residual bytes; memory headroom at 32K/64K/256K; exact token/logit plus GDN/QSA/Ple state parity; ordinary no-MTP route; and paired end-to-end samples under the official client. Keep measured current bandwidth separate from installed-link ceiling and historical transfer probe. The author's external results cannot substitute for these measurements.

## Reproducibility and sources

External sources were opened on 2026-10-13. Publication dates above come from the document/post metadata or venue named by the source. Retrieval was web-only; no clones or fetches were performed. The supplied registry file report-registry-v183.json881 did not exist at the given path during this run; local report review covered R45, R71 and R219, so candidate overlap with that registry remains unverified. No source or benchmark status was changed.
